extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, examiners, and students/practitioners seeking to understand EPC claim requirements
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for drafting and interpreting patent claims under the European Patent Convention (Article 84 and implementing Rules). Covers clarity, support, form (two-part claims), interpretation, and procedural aspects during search, examination and opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought (Article 84 EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 84 EPC: "The claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought. They shall be clear and concise and be supported by the description."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claims must set out what is being claimed (the purported invention). This ensures the public can determine what is and is not covered by the patent, providing legal certainty for third parties (e.g., for licensing, designing around, or market entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be clear and concise
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be clear (not obscure) and concise as required by Article 84 EPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law requires claims to be clear "in themselves when being read with the normal skills, but not including any knowledge derived from the description of the patent application" (i.e., clear in themselves). Ambiguity undermines legal certainty. Concision avoids unnecessary wording that can obscure scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be supported by the description
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 84 EPC requires that claims be supported by the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support means the scope of the claims must be justified by the disclosure in the description; a claim's scope must not extend beyond what the description and the technical contribution justify. This links claim breadth to the invention as disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must define the invention in terms of technical features
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must define the matter for which protection is sought in terms of the technical features of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical features may be structural (e.g., a nail, screw, rivet) or functional (e.g., fastening means). The claimed features should convey a technical teaching so the scope of protection can be assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be clear in themselves and not rely on the description to achieve clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Established case law: claims must be clear "in themselves" when read with normal skills; the skilled person's knowledge of the prior art may be used but not knowledge derived from the description to render an otherwise unclear claim clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is clear to the skilled person on its face, the description need not be consulted. Conversely, the description generally cannot be used to give a different meaning to a claim feature that has a clear technical meaning. Reference: decisions such as T 0908/04, T 454/89 and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of claims must not be broader than justified by the description and the contribution to the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the claims must not be "broader than is justified by the extent of the description and also the contribution to the art."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects the legal principle that the monopoly conferred by the claims should correspond to the technical contribution disclosed. Over-broad claims that claim more than the disclosed contribution are contrary to Article 84.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent claims should use two-part form where appropriate (Rule 43(1) EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 43(1) EPC imposes that an independent claim should be drafted in a two-part form: a preamble (pre-characterising portion) and a characterising part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble includes features that, in combination, are known from the closest prior art; the characterising part lists the features not known from that prior art. The two-part form should be used "wherever appropriate". A similar requirement exists in the PCT (Rule 6.3(b) PCT).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality of independent claims in the same category only in exceptional circumstances (Rule 43(2) EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 43(2) EPC allows more than one independent claim in the same category only in the exceptional circumstances listed in Rule 43(2)(a)-(c). The applicant bears the burden of showing that an exception applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 43(2) is applicable in examination proceedings (not in opposition). If multiple independent claims in the same category are present, the EPO may object under Rule 43(2) and require the applicant to indicate which claims should be searched/examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search-stage procedure under Rule 62a EPC for multiple independent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 62a EPC (since 1 April 2010) permits the EPO to invite the applicant to indicate, within two months, the claims complying with Rule 43(2) on the basis of which the search is to be carried out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant fails to indicate complying claims in time, the search is carried out on the basis of the first claim in each category. The applicant may contest a Rule 62a objection in reply to the search division or later before the examining division; the search division or examining division can revise the assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 84 EPC is not a ground for opposition or revocation; clarity may be examined post-amendment (G 3/14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 84 EPC is neither a ground of opposition under Article 100 EPC nor a ground for revocation under Article 138(1) EPC. However, Article 84 may be considered in opposition proceedings by virtue of Article 101(3) EPC if the patent proprietor amends the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Enlarged Board of Appeal in G 3/14 held that clarity of amended claims may be examined in opposition proceedings only when, and to the extent that, the amendment introduces non-compliance with Article 84. Prior lack of clarity in granted claims is not per se a ground for opposition/revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of claims: use of description for ambiguous terms; skilled-person standard and synthetical propensity
rubrics_metrics.description: In opposition/examination, if claims are sufficiently clear to a skilled person, there is no reason to consult the description. The description can be used as the patent's "dictionary" to assess the correct meaning of ambiguous claim terms, but it cannot be used to give a different meaning to a term that has a clear technical meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be interpreted through the eyes of the person skilled in the art, who should try—with synthetical propensity—to arrive at an interpretation that is technically meaningful and takes account of the whole disclosure. In case of discrepancy between clear claim wording and the description, the unambiguous claim wording is to be understood as the skilled person would without help of the description; description parts not reflected in the claims are generally not considered for novelty/inventive step assessments.
